title: [News] Small Batch, Premium Price: Could Tariffs Create a ‘Made in USA’ iPhone Category?
summary: Amid rising trade tensions and newly proposed tariffs, Apple is reportedly exploring limited iPhone production in the U.S. Producing low-volume, premium devices domestically could be practical as a symbolic gesture, though full-scale relocation would face major logistical hurdles and likely raise retail prices substantially.
content:
Q&A Assistant

TrendForce News operates independently from our research team, curating key semiconductor and tech updates to support timely, informed decisions.

The potential relocation of iPhone production to the U.S. has become a focal point amid escalating trade tensions and former President Trump’s newly proposed tariffs. According to a report from ijiwei, citing CNBC, Apple is reportedly exploring ways to shift part of its iPhone manufacturing to the U.S.

Currently, most iPhones are manufactured in China and India. The report notes that bringing iPhone production to the U.S. would pose significant challenges and could result in a substantial increase in retail prices.

Another possibility highlighted is producing a small volume of iPhones—or other niche products—in the U.S. This approach echoes Apple’s strategy during Trump’s first term, when the company assembled the high-end Mac Pro domestically. Producing low-volume, niche products in the U.S. is more practical and could serve as a symbolic move to appease political pressure, allowing Apple to claim some "Made in USA" manufacturing without a full supply-chain overhaul.

In February, Apple announced plans to invest USD 500 billion in the U.S. over the next four years, create 20,000 jobs, and build an AI server production facility in Houston, Texas. These commitments are part of broader efforts to bolster domestic operations and demonstrate investment in the American economy.

At the same time, Apple is actively diversifying its supply chain beyond China. Bloomberg reports the company assembled USD 22 billion worth of iPhones in India in the 12 months ending in March—representing a nearly 60% increase in production compared to the previous year. Such diversification suggests Apple is weighing multiple geographic strategies rather than a single, large-scale shift.

Whether small-batch, premium-priced U.S.-made iPhones become a reality will depend on policy pressures, cost trade-offs, and Apple’s willingness to absorb or pass on higher manufacturing prices. For now, limited domestic assembly remains the most feasible path to a "Made in USA" iPhone label.
